Came into this movie knowing it was classic, but it just doesn't feel like it hold up to modern standards. The visuals are outstanding, with wide shots of western scenery, big sets with tons of extras. The music is also iconic, even though I'd never seen this movie before the score is immediately recognizable. I can't really say anything good about the movie beyond that. The plot was boring, really nothing interesting about it. The acting wasn't great, or I just hated the characters. Maybe both. I kept thinking to myself that this felt like a bad Bollywood movie. High budget, over the top, unnecessarily long, poorly directed, and a bit cheesy. The audio even felt like it was a bad dub. At one point I had to check my video player's settings to make sure I was using the original audio it was so bad. For a movie to be centered around three characters, you really don't get to know them. They remain the same from the beginning to the end of the movie. Random plot points expound on the backgrounds of the character occasionally, but it's never meaningful. *Minor spoilers* When the Good and the Ugly are captured by Union soldiers, all of a sudden the Bad is a captain in the Union army. I kept thinking he had to have assumed someone's identity somehow or they would explain it further, but no. The man who is introduced in the beginning of the movie as an assassin who always kills his target once he's paid has somehow been a captain in the Union army this whole time. I usually like westerns, so to come out of this one so disappointed surprised me. This was a really hard movie to rate, because what it does well it does really well. What it doesn't do well, it really doesn't do well. It kind of reminds me of a lot of modern country music in a way, almost pandering to the audience without any substance. Overall, it falls short of being a good movie to me.

Great here we go again writing a review for another beloved classic that I didn’t dig. I need to hurry up and finish these classics so I can get back to watching what I actually want to. Three different parties all after some gold while war rages around them in the southwest is definitely an intense and fun setup. My favorite character is Angel Eyes and I wish he was in more of the movie. I like a lot of Tuco’s dialogue even if he’s very over the top. Blondie just has the cool factor instead of character development. He didn’t actually feel like “The Good” to me. I liked the war depictions. Scary stuff. I really like the setting and concept of the movie but a lot of the execution bugged me. I’m just going to list the stuff that bothered me and not go in depth because I don’t enjoy writing harsh thoughts on movies my friends love. -The biggest thing is the post-production dubbing. I found it incredibly distracting and wholly odd. -The gun store holdup didn’t make much sense to me. There’s zero precautions taken while handing someone a loaded gun. -I hate deus ex machina so the cannon saving Blondie annoyed me. -The movie is long and the pace is slow. -Tuco being chained to the guy holding him captive made no sense. It’s ridiculously unsafe and would be a huge hassle. -Angel Eyes not making Blondie a prisoner is stupid. He’s smart, evil, and aware that Blondie is a threat. As a whole I felt that Angel Eyes and Tuco were way too careless with Blondie. The lack of caution felt like lazy writing. -There’s a bunch of conveniences and liberties taken with Blondie and Tuco meeting up to take on Angel Eyes. Also where are the random explosions coming from in that scene? Are cannons just being shot randomly across the desert? -The exchange with the union captain felt completely strange and the dubbing played a really big part in that. It’s like they came up with the dialogue after the fact. -I found the standoff with the goons and the final standoff underwhelming. I wanted more thoughtfulness from the bad guys.

I'm beginning to feel that I'm more a fan of the revisionist and neo-westerns, that take the genre and stretch and shake out what it is and what it can be. This was a great disappointment after the brisk and entertaining Fistful of Dollars and absolutely did not need to be three hours long. Every moment when Tuco is on-screen is a crime against me. It feels like Leone engaged in his own self-parody, with a now much dumber Blondie and Tuco falling from shenanigan to shenanigan, they learn nothing and proceed to the next. I've read enough articles to see people analysing this film through the lens of the futility of war or the violence and cruelty of the Old West, but frankly, it offers such a simplistic and mean-spirited point of view that I just didn't enjoy its wanton brutality. There are some fantastic segments and cinematography in this (the climax, the bridge fight, the introduction of Angel Eyes, the walk through the desert and the church) but its interspersed by plodding, frustrating sections. It could've been great with a good edit, alas, it's clear Clint did this one for the money.

Фильм, очевидно, смотрится намного масштабнее предыдущих из "Долларовой трилогии". Локаций больше, яркие главные герои, интересная завязка, повышенные ставки в стиле классического вестерна — круто. И тем не менее, у меня больше неприятных впечатлений, чем приятных. Во время просмотра меня не покидало ощущение, что на экране я вижу незнакомых героев. Что главный герой трилогии, что полковник Дуглас нравились мне из-за своей человечности. Да, это дикий запад с дикими законами и разумеется, понятие морали тут очень растяжимо. Но это не мешает в главному герою в "За пригоршню долларов" по-доброму общаться с барменом и помогать семье, попавшей в беду. Это не мешает ему признать мастерство полковника Дугласа в "На несколько долларов больше", более того, подружиться с ним и вести дело вместе. В этом же фильме, герой Клинта Иствуда стал ухмыляющиймся отморозком, что меня очень расстроило. Да, сцена с исполнением мечты Капитана армии севера вроде как показывает его эмпатию, но вряд ли он бы стал взрывать тот мост, если бы сам в этом не нуждался. Так что им просто было по пути и он между делом угодил желаниям Капитана. В остальном главный герой хладнокровная пафосная и молчаливая картонка, и мне жаль это говорить. У него была своя, в каком-то смысле добрая харизма мальчишки-проныры, это подкупало. Ну да ладно, теперь о Дугласе. Во втором фильме он предстаёт перед зрителем как прагматичный, расчётливый профессионал с моральным кодексом или как минимум чувством чести. Опять же, он признал способности героя Иствуда и пошёл с ним на дело. Делился с ним переживаниями и опытом. Про его основную мотивацию я вообще молчу, желание отомстить за сестру это достаточно благородно (оставляем за скобками моральную сторону вопроса, опять же, это вестерн в котором важно зрелище). Здесь же, Дуглас тоже стал отморозком и это грустно. Получив власть в лагере армии севера он пользовался своим положением ради наживы, избивал людей и т.д. Но если оставить эмоции и попытаться трезво взглянуть на картину, то она выглядит вполне логично. В условиях отсутствия закона и морали люди меняются не в лучшую сторону, особенно ,когда на кону большие деньги. Особенно, когда на фоне идёт война. И вполне логично, что человечность героев стирается и остаются только атрибуты, по которым можно отличить друг от друга ожесточивчихся, расчеловеченых героев. Его не было в предыдущих фильмах, поэтому я изначально воспринимала его, как такого, жалкого жадного прохвоста. Отличный и яркий персонаж. Этот фильм вызвал во мне противоречивые эмоции, и это, на самом деле, здорово. Потому что я не написала ни слова о первых двух, хотя они мне понравились. Tengo que reconocer que el western no es un género que me atraiga especialmente y que, en ocasiones, puede llegar a hacérseme algo repetitivo, pero tenía una deuda con esta película y muchas ganas de verla, y he de decir que me ha dejado una sensación completamente distinta. A pesar de sus casi tres horas, no he sentido que se me hiciera realmente pesada, y eso me parece uno de sus mayores méritos, si bien es cierto que hay algún momento en el que el ritmo se resiente y algunas partes se podrían haber acortado. Leone se toma su tiempo, pero sabe perfectamente cómo utilizarlo. Cada plano, cada silencio, cada mirada y cada duelo están construidos con una clara intencionalidad. La película tiene una personalidad enorme, unos paisajes espectaculares (joder, qué bonita es España), una fotografía increíble y una puesta en escena que hace que hasta los momentos más pausados tengan algo que decir. Los tres protagonistas funcionan y se complementan ciertamente bien, y me ha dejado especialmente buen sabor de boca que ninguno sea el típico héroe o villano perfectamente definido, sino que todos se muevan por sus propios intereses y tengan su propia moral. Además, la banda sonora es absolutamente brutal y consigue elevar muchas escenas que ya de por sí funcionan, especialmente en el tramo final, donde se respira pura tensión hasta el último segundo. Una película que entiendo perfectamente que sea considerada un clásico.

I couldn’t predict a single thing that happened in this movie. This movie was so filled with energy and life to the point where I couldn’t even fathom somebody writing the story, the  entirety of the story just felt so unscripted, so natural, so sudden that every scene I was wondering, what are the writers gonna do here? Where can they take it from here? And I never ever had a clear answer. With modern movies it feels like I always know what the writer is planning to do next, but throughout this entire movie, I was just constantly flabbergasted at the concept that somebody sat down and thought of the story and wrote it down. Something else I’d like to mention that I noticed in this movie that when comparing it to modern media struck me as so fresh and new with the amount of quiet waiting, there was in this movie. This movie is full of moments where the characters wait and listen and think, where the actors truly get to shine and let their expressions speak for themselves. Which not only added to the realism of it all, but also opened up opportunities for so much more storytelling storytelling that felt much more deep and grounded and real. It feels like in modern movies the directors expect the audience to be stupid, they say everything so unbelievably clear. There is nothing expected of you, everything is just laid out clearly, but in this movie, a lot of the movie is just facial expressions, eye movements, little subtle hints of story that you have to pick up on on your own and I love it.

Laden with thematic depth and reflections on violence, relationships, money, and obviously the intersections of those three, The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly may be a little too long but it’s also far more emotionally engaging than the other films in the Dollars trilogy. Eli Wallach’s scenes around the halfway mark, convincing himself and Blondie both that he truly cares for him are an incredible showcase of talent and bring the film’s ideas into focus. When Clint Eastwood shows up in the town to help Tuco shoot his way through Angel Eyes’s crew of bandits, asking him “Were you gonna die alone?” the bizarro brotherhood between these characters is crystal clear. They love each other, they have each other’s backs, but Tuco in particular can’t stop himself from stabbing Blondie in the back. Blondie knows this, and just accepts that that’s the way it is - he treats Tuco accordingly. From there we move to the bridge sequence, as pointed a war satire as there ever was, and finally, what is probably, for my money, the greatest sequence in movie history, the cemetery. With a bit more research and a couple of ancillary texts, I could probably write a few thousand words on the overwhelming scale of the setting and the goal of the characters in being there. My final (and initial) thoughts on this movie are that this is not Sergio Leone, Clint Eastwood, Lee Van Cleef, or even Eli Wallach’s movie (although he has quite a claim to it). It’s Ennio Morricone’s. Every single scene is not just elevated by the music, it’s made by it. This score is so perfect, so tonally dialed-in, that it carries the movie even more than John Williams’s work on The Empire Strikes Back does. Of course, in the case of Star Wars , the music doesn’t need to support every scene in the same way. In a movie like this one, with sparse dialogue and beautiful yet largely unexciting visuals, the music is able to be the main character. It fits each scene like off-the-rack pants fit a 5’10”, 160lb white man - that is to say, nothing has ever fit better. It’s considered one of the best of all time for a reason, but it really does stand out as exceptional in an already incredible movie.

The film begins by introducing its three main characters. And it does it so brilliantly that it might just have one of the greatest character introductions in cinema history. Clint Eastwood plays the Good — Blondie, as he is called in the film. Lee Van Cleef plays the Bad — Angel Eyes. And Eli Wallach plays the Ugly — Tuco. Although all three performances are excellent, Eli Wallach's performance as Tuco is easily my favorite. He gets more screen time than the other two, but more importantly, somehow manages to become incredibly likable despite being, well… Tuco. Coming from extreme poverty, Tuco has embraced banditry and has absolutely no idea what morality even means. He's selfish, greedy, opportunistic, and constantly looking for the easiest way to make money. Blondie, on the other hand, is a lone wolf who lives by his own rules. And then there's Angel Eyes — compared to the other two, he's more refined and knows exactly how to position himself alongside whoever holds the power. During the Civil War, for example, he rises to the rank of colonel and uses the army to further his own interests. In that sense, the three characters can almost be seen as three different social types: The Bad is disciplined, military, and part of the system. The Good is a scruffy outsider who refuses to belong to any system. The Ugly is essentially a poor man from the countryside who has chosen banditry and is desperately looking for a shortcut to wealth. And that's what makes the three characters so interesting: these aren't just Western archetypes. They're three types of people we can still recognize around us today.
